entries.title: Phase-aware metal-ligand and redox speciation
entries.use_when: An inorganic reaction or equation-selection problem requires product identification, balancing, coefficient-derived quantities, or exact evaluation of structural transformation claims.
steps: Establish credible products from conditions and chemical constraints before treating an atom-balanced equation as chemically established.
Balance atoms and charge, then reduce the full equation to the smallest whole-number coefficient vector.
Label reactant-side, product-side, and full-equation coefficient sets; apply sums, products, or ratios only to the set explicitly named by the wording.
For transformation claims, distinguish bonds or groups newly formed by the operation from features already present and merely retained.
Audit every statement against the same equation and transformation ledger, then check uniqueness before selecting a single-best or catch-all response.
guards: Atom balance alone does not validate guessed product identities.
The mathematical product of all coefficients includes both sides unless the wording explicitly restricts the scope.
Normalize coefficients before computing any coefficient aggregate.
Retention of an existing structural feature is not evidence that the stated transformation generated it.

entries.title: Fixed-volume real-gas enthalpy change
retrieval_terms: fixed volume van der Waals enthalpy
real gas delta H delta PV
entries.use_when: A closed real gas at fixed amount and volume receives heat or changes temperature and the requested quantity is enthalpy rather than internal energy.
steps: Use the fixed-volume heat as the internal-energy change only when the stated process justifies it.
Compute enthalpy from delta H equals delta U plus delta of PV, evaluating each pressure from the stated equation of state.
Apply pressure-volume unit conversion once and report the final enthalpy with its sign and requested units.
guards: Do not stop at heat input when the question asks for enthalpy.
Do not discard covolume or attraction terms without checking their cancellation under the stated constraints.

entries.title: Monatomic ideal-gas absolute molar entropy
entries.use_when: A monatomic ideal gas absolute entropy is requested from temperature, pressure or volume, and particle or molar mass.
steps: Convert mass to the per-particle quantity required by the translational partition expression and keep SI units throughout.
Use the volume-per-particle or equivalent pressure form consistently, including the additive five-halves term.
Convert the per-particle entropy to molar entropy and report joules per mole-kelvin.
guards: Do not insert molar mass directly where single-particle mass is required.
Do not omit Planck-constant powers or mix pressure and volume forms.

entries.title: Immediate response to corrosive chemical exposure
retrieval_terms: corrosive skin eye exposure first aid
entries.use_when: A visible option set asks for the first response to acid, alkali, caustic, or other corrosive contact with skin or eyes.
steps: Prioritize immediate copious water rinsing, flushing, or safety-shower use and removal of contaminated material when stated.
Choose the option that starts decontamination promptly, then follow the requested medical or site procedure.
guards: Do not neutralize a corrosive directly on tissue because the reaction and delay can worsen injury.
Reject covering, drying, waiting, oil or lotion, and soap-only responses when immediate flushing is available.

entries.title: Reversible isothermal heat entropy
retrieval_terms: reversible isothermal heat entropy q over T
entropy change heat transfer constant temperature
entries.use_when: Use when a chemistry or physical-chemistry problem asks for entropy change from reversible heat transfer at a specified constant temperature.
steps: Convert heat to joules and temperature to kelvin before calculating entropy.
Use Delta S = q_rev / T for the object whose entropy change is requested, preserving the sign of heat flow.
Report the requested units and keep any required separate final-answer line.
guards: Do not use Celsius directly in the denominator, drop the heat-flow sign, or treat irreversible path heat as q_rev unless the problem supplies reversible/equilibrium heat.

entries.title: Nitrate/nitrite chemistry and dual-mechanism toxicity
entries.use_when: A nitrate or nitrite question asks about chemical role, toxicity mechanism, or a symptom pattern that may combine impaired oxygen transport with cardiovascular effects.
steps: Distinguish direct nitrite exposure from nitrate exposure that first requires biological conversion to nitrite.
Model nitrite toxicity with both hemoglobin oxidation to methemoglobin and vascular smooth-muscle relaxation rather than using either mechanism alone.
Map methemoglobinemia to impaired oxygen delivery and cyanosis, and map vasodilation to reduced blood pressure with compensatory tachycardia; allow these findings to overlap at low exposure.
Compare each candidate symptom bundle against the combined mechanism and stated severity, using toxicant-specific evidence instead of equating a generic severity label with an asymptomatic stage.
guards: Do not collapse nitrite intoxication into a methemoglobin-percentage table alone.
Do not assume mild intoxication means symptomless unless exposure or clinical data establish that stage.
Do not transfer direct-nitrite effects unchanged to nitrate without checking route and conversion context.

entries.title: Photophysics Color Energy Direction
entries.use_when: A question asks for emitted, observed, or absorbed visible color from photon energy, wavelength, or conjugated-dye wording.
steps: Convert photon energy to wavelength, or use the given emitted or observed color only after identifying the requested direction.
If the prompt asks absorbed color after giving dye emission, choose the complementary absorbed band instead of repeating the emitted band.
When visible choices include colors with numeric wavelength labels, use the chemically requested color relation first and treat labels as secondary checks.
resources: L3_functions/electromagnetic_energy_tools.py when a numeric photon conversion is useful
guards: Keep emitted, observed, transmitted, and absorbed color directions distinct.
Do not let a numeric value printed beside a choice override an explicit absorbed-versus-emitted relation.

entries.title: Inorganic Gas Trap Stoichiometry
retrieval_terms: inorganic gas drying absorbent red hot copper stoichiometry
ammonium nitrite nitrate decomposition nitrous oxide copper
calcium hydroxide carbon dioxide perchlorate drying gas
entries.use_when: Gas-analysis or inorganic decomposition tasks pass products through drying, carbon dioxide absorption, red-hot copper, or STP volume and pressure measurements.
steps: Identify which trap removes water, which removes carbon dioxide, and whether red-hot copper consumes an oxidizing gas while leaving nitrogen.
Balance source decomposition equations and any copper oxidation equation before converting trap mass gains to moles.
Use residual gas volume, pressure, and temperature on a consistent basis to close the mole balance.
Report the requested mole ratio, composition, or visible choice only after checking all trapped and untrapped gas streams.
guards: Do not treat every mass increase as water; match each trap to the species it retains or reacts with.
Check whether an oxide-forming gas is consumed before assigning the residual gas identity.

entries.title: Michael Enolate Product Pair Matching
retrieval_terms: beta keto ester vinyl sulfoxide cyclopentylidene ester
sodium ethoxide sodium hydride conjugate addition
entries.use_when: A reaction asks for ordered major products from enolate conjugate addition or a Michael-type pair using visible structures or names.
steps: Identify each substrate pair, the enolate donor, conjugate acceptor, base, and likely conjugate-addition site.
Compare visible choices by both ordered product connectivities, penalizing regioisomer, succinate, or simple substitution distractors.
guards: Do not reuse a letter mapping when the choices are relettered or reordered.

entries.title: Diels-Alder bridged-product face and descriptor audit
entries.use_when: A Diels-Alder product choice requires connectivity, endo or exo assignment, or named and R/S-defined stereochemistry for a bridged adduct, including ordinary cyclopentadiene with a monosubstituted electron-poor alkene.
steps: Map diene and dienophile atoms into the completed product skeleton, preserve the diene internal bond and dienophile relationships, and number the actual bridged framework before assigning stereochemistry; a group directed toward the highest-numbered bridge is exo and one directed away is endo, while any separate diene-face preference remains an independent axis.

Draw one internally consistent three-dimensional adduct, then assign priorities and R/S independently at each listed center by following complete ring paths on the final graph rather than translating an endo label into a memorized descriptor tuple.

As a checked calibration for an otherwise unsubstituted norborn-5-ene-2-carboxylate alkyl ester, the endo pair is (1R,2R,4R)/(1S,2S,4S), whereas the exo pair is (1R,2S,4R)/(1S,2R,4S); changing the ester O-alkyl group does not change the ring-center assignments.
Recognize the enantiomeric partner expected from achiral reactants and distinguish global inversion from a single-center mismatch.
Compare each option as a full feature vector of connectivity, bridge orientation, retained relationships, endo or exo geometry, and every descriptor before selecting it.
guards: Do not translate endo or exo directly into a memorized R/S tuple; for the conventional norborn-5-ene-2-carboxylate calibration, do not swap the endo and exo C2 descriptor while keeping the same bridgehead enantiomer.
Do not equate endo or exo with a separate syn or anti facial preference.
Recompute priorities on the product graph because the two ring paths can rank differently than visual intuition suggests.
Check global inversion before treating two absolute descriptor sets as different constitutional or relative-stereochemical products.

entries.title: Peroxide-former recognition, concentration hazards, and response
entries.use_when: A safety or mechanism question links air exposure, evaporation, purification, or distillation to explosion, especially for oximes or other peroxide-forming organics, and candidate answers mix a broad reaction class with a more specific causal pathway.
steps: Identify the exact reactive class and distinguish peroxide formation from unrelated oxidizer incompatibility; for oximes, distinguish aldehyde-derived from ketone-derived members when relevant.

Build the causal chain: oxygen exposure can form peroxide species, evaporation or distillation can concentrate less-volatile energetic impurities and add heat, and peroxide decomposition can initiate an explosion.

Rank candidate mechanisms by causal specificity. When generic oxidation and a specific peroxide-generating pathway are both offered, use the specific pathway if it directly explains the stated concentration or distillation hazard.

Check alternatives against their necessary conditions: hydrolysis requires an appropriate aqueous pathway, polymerization requires polymerizable functionality or a documented alert, and generic oxidation alone does not identify the energetic impurity.
Normalize recognizable spelling variants during reasoning, then preserve the requested answer representation.
guards: Do not treat a specific peroxide-forming pathway and its umbrella oxidation class as independent competing mechanisms.
Do not infer that every oxidizable organic compound is a peroxide former; require class-specific or substance-specific evidence.
Keep peroxide formation separate from its later concentration, heating, and initiation during processing.
For handling recommendations, defer to authoritative substance-specific safety guidance rather than mechanism alone.

entries.title: Qualitative inorganic reaction-network deduction
entries.use_when: Unlabeled aqueous samples, including prepared mixtures, must be identified from linked precipitate, gas, redox, and directed excess-reagent observations.
steps: Define sample domains, stock-use, concentration, internal-stability constraints, and latent product and gas variables.
For each observation, build the complete relation over sample compositions, product identity, gas identity, and directed excess behavior; include all compatible composite-mixture candidates.
Join relations that share samples or claim the same product, then enforce global stock-use and stability constraints until arc consistency reaches a fixed point.
Backtrack only if domains remain non-singleton; record the surviving global-assignment count and exact elimination reason after every join.
Return all solutions, the forced-component intersection, possible-component union, explicit alternatives, and a minimum contradictory subset when no solution exists.
guards: Do not assign an identity before its complete local candidate relation is represented.
Treat same-precipitate claims as equality of product identity, not merely equality of color.
Preserve the stated direction of excess-reagent and sequential-addition tests.
Do not force an exact assignment when the joined system has zero or multiple solutions.

entries.title: Empirical compatibility-table hazard disambiguation
entries.use_when: A safety question asks for empirical hazard categories produced by pairing broad chemical reactivity classes, especially legacy EPA chemical-storage or hazardous-waste compatibility groups.
steps: Preserve the exact class pair, roles, physical forms, and qualifiers.
Treat requested categories as empirical pair outputs rather than consequences inferred from generic reactivity.
For legacy EPA names, call hazardous_waste_compatibility.lookup_chemical_storage_compatibility with both visible class names.
Decode only returned codes and assess heat, fire, explosion, gas formation, and polymerization independently.
Translate supported categories only after classification; a blank chart cell means unknown, not safe.
guards: Do not select a category without exact-pair evidence.
Heat, fire, and explosion are distinct categories.
Reject neighboring classes and member-specific substitutions.
A blank chart cell is not evidence of compatibility.

entries.title: Evidence-ranked transformation balance and aromaticity checks
entries.use_when: A structure or reaction question compares HX-release stoichiometry, aromatization, or π-electron claims after ring opening, elimination, or rearrangement, especially for gem-dihalocyclopropane or fused-ring substrates.
steps: Map the visible structure or SMILES into rings and bonds, marking the attachment and possible fate of every halogen rather than counting halogen atoms alone.

For an indene-derived gem-dihalocyclopropane, consider ring opening followed by aromatizing loss of one HX while the other halogen remains in the fused aromatic product; confirm the actual coefficient by balancing substrate, product, and HX.

Identify the exact cyclic conjugated circuit named by each claim, verify cyclicity, planarity, and continuous conjugation, then count unique π electrons and apply 4n+2; distinguish a six-electron benzene-like circuit from the total count of a larger fused system.
Evaluate every candidate independently and prefer atom-balanced or directly structure-derived claims over exact supramolecular topology or contact counts unsupported by the supplied structure.
guards: Never equate the number of substrate halogens with the number of HX molecules released.
Do not mix a local ring-circuit π count with the unique-electron count of an entire fused aromatic system.
Do not require lowercase aromatic SMILES notation; a Kekule-form alternating ring may sanitize as aromatic.
Do not infer exact hydrogen-bond dimensionality or contact counts from viscosity behavior or incomplete structural evidence.

entries.title: Coupled back-titration and cross-standardization balance
entries.use_when: A back-titration uses one unknown reagent concentration while a separate standardization relates that concentration to another unknown titrant concentration.
steps: Assign each concentration and volume its physical role and experiment, convert volumes consistently, and obtain equivalent factors from balanced reactions.
Write the separate standardization relation as νA·CA·VA = νB·CB·VB, retaining it as a relation between concentrations.
Write the main balance: initial reagent equivalents equal analyte equivalents consumed plus residual reagent equivalents measured by the back titration.
Substitute the standardization relation into the main balance, solve the requested concentration, and postpone rounding until the final output.
Back-substitute into both balances; require positive quantities, matching equivalent totals, correct dimensions, and the requested answer format.
guards: Keep volumes from separate experiments attached to their original physical roles.
Do not omit the analyte equivalent factor or invert the standardization volume ratio.
A back-titrant measures residual reagent; its equivalents are not additional analyte consumption.
Do not accept a numeric result until both independent balances reproduce it.

entries.title: Real-gas compressibility model and virial-order selection
entries.use_when: A real-gas problem requests a compressibility factor from state data or asks for a virial approximation derived from an equation of state.
steps: Declare whether the target is the observed-state definition, a density virial truncation, a pressure virial truncation, or the full equation of state before substituting values.
For the van der Waals equation, derive the second virial coefficient B2(T)=b-a/(RT).
For a first pressure-form virial estimate, use Z≈1+B2(T)p/(RT); retain additional terms only when the requested order supports them.
Use Z=pV_m/(RT), with V_m=M/rho when needed, for the supplied-state factor or as an independent consistency check.
Report the dimensionless result from the requested model and verify units, expansion variable, and truncation order.
guards: Do not silently replace a virial truncation with the exact van der Waals equation.
Do not mix pressure-form p/(RT) with density-form 1/V_m corrections.
Do not force every supplied constant into the calculation.
Do not let a consistency check override an explicitly requested approximation.

entries.title: Addition-mechanism selectivity disambiguation
entries.use_when: An organic addition question asks why one product is observed or compares concertedness, stereospecificity, syn/anti addition, rearrangement, regiochemistry, and temperature effects.
steps: List the alternatives that could multiply products: constitutional or regioisomers, rearranged skeletons, stereoisomers, and conformers; identify which type the observation excludes.
Classify the mechanism as concerted, carbocation-mediated, radical, or cyclic-intermediate, then determine whether rearrangement or competing 1,2/1,4 pathways are available.

For hydroboration, use the four-center concerted addition to exclude a free carbocation and ordinary hydride or alkyl shifts; treat syn addition and chiral-reagent facial control as separate consequences.

Test each explanation for sufficiency: stereospecific or syn behavior constrains relative stereochemistry but does not by itself eliminate regioisomers, constitutional products, or enantiomeric alternatives.
Use temperature diagnostically: changing product ratios supports competing kinetic and thermodynamic pathways, whereas invariance is an observation that still needs a mechanistic cause.
guards: Do not infer a unique product from stereospecific, stereoselective, or syn without checking connectivity and regiochemistry.
Do not infer uniqueness from concertedness alone; verify symmetry, facial selectivity, and other concerted pathways.
Do not use an unrelated pericyclic-reaction retrieval hit as support for alkene hydroboration.

entries.title: Stagewise phosphorus stereochemistry and 31P NMR environment counting
entries.use_when: A reaction-monitoring or structure question asks how proton-decoupled phosphorus NMR signal counts change as substituents at tetrahedral phosphorus are replaced or hydrolyzed.
steps: Draw the phosphorus substituent set at each named stage and determine constitution, charge or protonation, symmetry, and exchange on the NMR timescale before counting signals.

When tetrahedral phosphorus has four nonequivalent ligand paths, enumerate its configurations; with fixed stereocenters or a chiral environment, opposite phosphorus configurations are diastereomeric and may give separate resonances.

After hydrolysis to an ordinary phosphate diester monoanion, treat the two nonbridging oxygens as equivalent through delocalized charge and bonding; phosphorus configurational chirality is lost unless isotopic or elemental substitution distinguishes those oxygens.
Count chemically distinct phosphorus environments at each endpoint, separate signal count from chemical-shift movement, and only then map the direction of change to the requested answer.
Treat simultaneous reactant and product resonances at partial conversion as a transient mixture rather than the endpoint pattern.
guards: Do not infer resonance count from stereoisomer count alone: enantiomers coincide in an achiral medium, whereas diastereomers can separate.
Proton decoupling removes scalar splitting by protons; it does not merge chemically nonequivalent phosphorus environments.
Do not freeze one Lewis form of a phosphate anion and treat its nonbridging oxygens as different.
Flag unusual pH, isotopic labeling, slow exchange, aggregation, or incomplete conversion when these could change the observed pattern.

entries.title: Particle-balance ionization from colligative data
entries.use_when: A freezing-point, boiling-point, or osmotic measurement is used to infer the fraction or percentage of a weak electrolyte that ionizes or dissociates.
steps: Compute solute molality from moles per kilogram of solvent and use the positive magnitude of the colligative change.
Infer the observed van't Hoff factor from deltaTf/(Kf*m), deltaTb/(Kb*m), or osmotic pressure/(MRT), then check its physical range.
Write the ionization event actually being measured, count nu product particles per ionized formula unit, and use i = (1-alpha) + nu*alpha = 1 + alpha*(nu-1).
Solve alpha = (i-1)/(nu-1); for one sequential weak-acid ionization, nu = 2 even when the parent acid has additional ionizable protons.
Convert alpha to percent, round only at the end, and verify by reconstructing both i and the measured colligative change.
guards: Do not equate the number of acidic protons with nu unless complete simultaneous dissociation is explicit.
If several sequential ionizations materially contribute, one measured i constrains only the average particle increase and cannot uniquely recover every stepwise fraction.
Use kilograms of solvent rather than solution mass when calculating molality.
Require 0 <= alpha <= 1 and back-substitute into the original colligative equation.

entries.title: Quantitative halogen isotope-envelope comparison
entries.use_when: A mass-spectrum problem infers counts of chlorine, bromine, or other two-isotope atoms from reported M, M+2, M+4, or higher cluster intensities.
steps: Identify which reported peak is normalized to 100 and express every observed intensity with that same denominator.
For each candidate composition, form the isotope generating polynomial; for chlorine and bromine use (p_light+p_heavy*x) raised to each atom count, where the coefficient of x^k represents M+2k.
Use supplied or tabulated natural-abundance fractions when candidates are close, expand the polynomial, and normalize its coefficients to the stated reference peak.
Compare all reported peaks quantitatively, rank candidates by residual error, and inspect the predicted cluster length and terminal peaks without treating unreported peaks as absent.
If alternatives remain within the measurement precision, report the ambiguity; otherwise select only after the numerical comparison.
guards: Do not sum heavy-isotope percentages across multiple atoms; use binomial or multinomial coefficients.
Do not compare percentages normalized to different peaks.
Do not let rounded 3:1 or 1:1 mnemonics decide a near tie when abundance-based calculation is available.
Do not assume an unreported M, M+6, or terminal peak is absent.

entries.title: Protein IEX selection from sequence to empirical screening
entries.use_when: A protein ion-exchange chromatography problem asks for the starting information, exchanger polarity, matrix-selection sequence, or distinction between initial design and later optimization.
steps: Identify whether the prompt asks for the earliest design input, an exchanger choice, or a later experimental optimization step.
When the protein sequence is known, estimate its theoretical pI as the initial charge descriptor; if sequence and pI are unavailable, use measured pI or structured screening as the fallback.
Compare a protein-compatible operating pH with pI: above pI the protein is net negative and favors an anion exchanger; below pI it is net positive and favors a cation exchanger.
After forming the charge-based exchanger hypothesis, empirically screen resin chemistries, pH, conductivity or salt, binding, and elution before preparative scale-up.
For first-step wording, choose the earliest prerequisite information or prediction rather than a downstream screen or column run.
guards: Do not reverse exchanger nomenclature: anion exchangers are positively charged and bind anionic proteins; cation exchangers are negatively charged and bind cationic proteins.
Treat predicted pI as a starting heuristic, not proof of binding; surface charge, tags, post-translational modifications, stability, impurities, and conductivity can alter practical behavior.
Avoid operating too near pI without justification because weak net charge and aggregation can undermine binding.
If sequence or pI is genuinely unavailable, empirical screening may become the first practical step; follow the stated information and objective.

entries.title: Positional substituent effects on aromatic carbonyl IR
entries.use_when: Comparing carbonyl stretching frequencies among regioisomeric aromatic aldehydes or ketones bearing the same ring substituent.
steps: Parse each structure first and label the substituent as ortho, meta, or para relative to the carbonyl-bearing ring carbon.
Because the compared carbonyls have essentially the same reduced mass, rank changes in their effective force constant rather than applying a molecular-mass heuristic.
Consider field/inductive, resonance-transmission, and ortho-specific conformational or through-space effects separately; no single electron-withdrawal or steric slogan determines every ordering.
For nitro-substituted aromatic aldehyde reference-trend questions, apply the experimentally established carbonyl-stretch series ortho < para < meta as an empirical class fact.
Establish the compound sequence before mapping it to the requested answer format.
guards: Never rank an ortho isomer from steric deconjugation alone.
Do not generalize the nitro/aldehyde empirical sequence to every substituent or carbonyl class.
Explicit solvent, phase, conformer, or measured-band data override a generic class trend.
Determine the chemistry ordering before inspecting option labels.

entries.title: Reciprocal-rate axis choice for reactor arrangements
retrieval_terms: ideal reactor sequence rate concentration curve
entries.use_when: Use when selecting or comparing an arrangement of ideal reactor units from rate plots, especially when candidate methods differ by concentration versus conversion axes or by sizing versus sequencing purpose.
steps: Classify the task first: sizing a reactor at a target conversion and sequencing a fixed set of reactor units are related but distinct design questions.

For the classic single-reaction sequencing heuristic, express the positive reciprocal disappearance rate as a function of reactant concentration and use the curve shape to identify orderings that retain favorable-rate concentration regions.

Use a conversion-axis plot only after deriving the concentration-conversion mapping from the material balance and accounting for volumetric-flow or density changes; preserve axis direction and any Jacobian needed for area arguments.
Match each proposed method to the requested design purpose and stated assumptions instead of selecting a plot solely from its familiar name.
Check the sequence qualitatively against the rate curve: it should avoid unnecessary reactor volume in high reciprocal-rate regions.
guards: Do not treat a conversion-based sizing plot as automatically interchangeable with a concentration-state arrangement plot.
Do not assume C_A = C_A0(1-X_A) unless constant volumetric flow is justified.
Use -r_A as a positive disappearance rate and keep concentration and conversion axis directions distinct.
A temperature profile is not a universal sequencing criterion unless nonisothermal effects are explicitly part of the design.

entries.title: Coupled solubility, precipitation, and acid-base regression
entries.use_when: Solubility or precipitation is coupled to pH, buffering, protonation, or complexation, including threshold precipitation calculations and multi-point measurements used to recover equilibrium constants.
steps: Write the solubility product, relevant acid-base equilibria, stoichiometric exponents, and mass balances together; distinguish free-ion concentrations from total dissolved concentration.

For threshold precipitation, use the target free-metal concentration to obtain the required hydroxide concentration, convert to pH or pOH, solve the buffer ratio, and then apply final volume and molar mass to the requested reagent amount.

For multi-point solubility data, derive the transformed model before fitting; for a 1:1 salt with a protonatable anion, fit squared solubility against hydrogen-ion concentration, with intercept Ksp and slope Ksp/Ka.

Transform observations without premature rounding, compute centered-sum ordinary least squares, recover physical constants algebraically, and check positivity, residual quality, and limiting behavior.

Retain guard digits and accept a printed numerical choice only when the unrounded result lies within its displayed rounding interval; evaluate underlying statements independently before selecting a multiple-correct response.
guards: Respect every stoichiometric exponent in the solubility product.
Do not replace a free-ion concentration with total solubility when protonation or complexation is present.
Do not mix pre-dilution and final-volume concentration bases.
Do not regress directly against pH when the derived variable is hydrogen-ion concentration.
Do not estimate fitted coefficients from endpoints or use answer choices as regression targets.
Do not treat numerical proximity as valid rounding equivalence.

entries.title: Role-scoped physical quantity binding
entries.use_when: A quantitative chemistry problem supplies a concentration that could denote molecules, reactive groups, or the concentration variable of an integrated rate law, especially in step-growth kinetics.
steps: Label every concentration by species and basis, then write the governing rate law and the units of its rate constant before converting anything.
For stoichiometric bifunctional step growth, obtain conversion from Xn=1/(1-p), so p=1-1/Xn.
For equal-concentration second-order kinetics, set ct=c0(1-p)=c0/Xn and use t=(1/ct-1/c0)/k=(Xn-1)/(k*c0), optionally through second_order_time.

Use the problem-supplied initial concentration directly when it is the concentration variable of the stated or standard integrated law; apply a functionality factor only when a different molecular or group basis is explicitly defined and the rate constant uses that same basis.
Check units and back-substitute the result into 1+k*c0*t=Xn.
guards: Do not multiply a supplied concentration by monomer functionality from the monomer label alone.
Never combine a molecule-based concentration with a functional-group-based rate constant or rate law.
Treat successful tool execution as evidence only; verify argument basis, units, and back-substitution.

entries.title: Answer representation, scaling, tolerance adjudication, and provenance
entries.use_when: A quantitative chemistry multiple-choice problem provides numeric choices, an explicit error or rounding tolerance, or a catch-all choice.
steps: Derive each requested physical quantity independently of the options and retain unrounded guard digits.
Identify whether the acceptance rule is absolute or relative, percent or percentage points, and strict or inclusive.
For every option expressing the same quantity and units, compute the required deviation from the unrounded result; evaluate every relevant quantity when choices mix properties or analytes.
Select a numeric option only if it satisfies the cutoff; if none does and a catch-all choice exists, select the catch-all rather than the nearest value.
Return the requested answer format and, when useful, state the decisive deviation-versus-cutoff comparison.
guards: Never round the calculated reference value before applying the tolerance test.
Nearest is not equivalent to within tolerance.
Do not confuse relative percent error with absolute error or percentage-point difference.
Compare only options representing the same physical quantity and units.

entries.title: Diastereotopic methylene protons and NMR multiplicity
entries.use_when: A proton-NMR or structure problem contains a CH2 near a stereogenic element, asks whether its two hydrogens are equivalent, or asks for their individual multiplicities.
steps: Fix the complete structure and stereochemical state, then use the shared proton-equivalence and coupling core to apply the substitution test and NMR-timescale checks.
Treat nonequivalent methylene hydrogens as separate spins and list geminal, vicinal, and longer-range couplings for each proton.
Use a doublet-of-doublets description only for resolved first-order unequal couplings; use AB or ABX language when chemical-shift separation is comparable to J.
guards: Do not call hydrogens diastereotopic merely because a chiral center is nearby; apply the substitution test to the actual structure.
Do not combine geminal and vicinal partners into one n+1 neighbor count.
Do not claim every diastereotopic CH2 must display two resolved peaks or a clean doublet of doublets.
Do not confuse diastereotopic with enantiotopic substitution outcomes.

entries.title: Stagewise organic structure tracking to product or proton multiplicity
entries.use_when: A multistep organic product or spectroscopy problem combines carbocation rearrangement, elimination or alkene cleavage, and carbonyl cyclization, making the result depend on propagated connectivity and competing ring closures.
steps: Label the starting carbon skeleton and maintain an atom-and-connectivity ledger after every reagent, recording each broken bond, formed bond, charge, and migrated substituent.

At each carbocation, iteratively enumerate feasible 1,2-hydride, alkyl, and ring-bond shifts before capture; retain shifts that improve cation stability or relieve meaningful ring strain and redraw the full skeleton.
For elimination and alkene cleavage, identify the actual beta hydrogen and leaving group, then convert each alkene carbon separately to an aldehyde or ketone according to its retained substituents.

For a dicarbonyl, list every alpha carbon that bears hydrogen and pair it with each electrophilic carbonyl; count the prospective ring as the atoms on the existing path between those two carbons, endpoints included.

Compare feasible closures, normally favoring five- or six-membered rings under reversible conditions; draw the beta-hydroxy carbonyl, reverse-cleave its new bond, and verify carbon and functional-group conservation.
guards: Do not trap the first carbocation before checking whether sequential rearrangements remain favorable.
Do not infer a new ring size from dicarbonyl locants; count the atoms on the closing path.
Do not assume the least hindered alpha site wins when reversible enolization and ring topology favor another closure.
Reject a proposed product unless retro-aldol cleavage and atom balance recover the mapped precursor.

entries.title: NMR experiment selection by nucleus and diagnostic contrast
entries.use_when: An NMR planning or multiple-choice task asks which experiment best distinguishes structures differing in stereochemistry, substitution, or a heteronuclear probe environment.
steps: Identify the structural difference and list the spin-active nuclei whose local environments or couplings it changes.

Rank direct observation of an affected, sensitive, well-dispersed nucleus highly; fluorine-19 is especially informative when fluorine environments differ because it has full natural abundance, high sensitivity, and broad chemical-shift dispersion.

Match the alternative experiments to their actual information channels: proton spectra report proton environments, HMBC reports long-range bond connectivity, and NOESY reports specific through-space proton contacts.

Choose NOESY for stereochemical discrimination only when a concrete diagnostic proton-proximity contrast is expected; otherwise prefer the simplest direct experiment with the clearest predicted spectral difference.
State the predicted distinguishing feature and why the nearest alternative is less direct or more ambiguous.
guards: Do not choose NOESY merely because the prompt mentions stereochemistry.
Do not choose a heteronuclear experiment solely because that element is present; verify that the compared structures change its environment or coupling pattern.
Enantiomers ordinarily have identical spectra in an achiral medium; require a chiral medium, derivatization, or another chiral discrimination mechanism.
Account for symmetry and conformational averaging before claiming distinct shifts, couplings, or NOE contacts.

entries.title: Exact tabulated periodic-property disambiguation
entries.use_when: An element-ranking or multiple-choice task depends on an exact named periodic-property scale, especially for transition metals or candidate ties.
steps: Identify the named property and scale, then express each option as ordering and equality constraints.
Search exact-value knowledge; if absent, search tools for a matching property lookup before ending retrieval.
Require supported values for every element from one consistent scale and reject missing or sentinel values.
Compare at the source precision, preserve supported ties, and map the resulting relation exactly to the visible option.
If exact support remains unavailable, use broad trends only to eliminate contradictions and lower confidence rather than inventing values.
guards: Across-period trends are not reliably monotonic within transition metals.
Never interpret zero or unknown from an incomplete property table as a measured value.
Do not create ties by mixing scales or incompatible reporting precision.

entries.title: Cannizzaro eligibility with competing carbonyl pathways
entries.use_when: Counting or classifying aldehydes that can undergo Cannizzaro chemistry, especially α-branched or multifunctional carbonyl structures.
steps: Inventory every aldehyde and every other enolizable carbonyl; count α-hydrogens at each site and identify possible enolate donors and aldehyde acceptors.
Treat an aldehyde with no α-hydrogen as an ordinary Cannizzaro candidate; direct attachment of the formyl carbon to an aromatic ring normally satisfies this screen.
For an isolated R2CH–CHO aldehyde with one α-hydrogen, consider the established exception in which aldol formation consumes the last α-H and a subsequent crossed-Cannizzaro step remains accessible.

Before applying that exception to a multifunctional molecule, enumerate intramolecular enolate attacks; a pathway closing a favorable five- or six-membered ring onto the aldehyde makes aldol cyclization the controlling classification.
Assign one verdict per compound after resolving all sites and competing pathways, then map the resulting count to the requested answer format.
guards: Do not treat exactly one α-hydrogen as unconditional Cannizzaro eligibility.
Do not inspect only the aldehyde α-carbon in a polycarbonyl molecule; audit every enolizable site and feasible ring closure.
Do not let broad “can undergo” wording license hypothetical trace or nonstandard pathways when an established competing reaction controls the classification.
Count compounds rather than aldehyde groups unless the prompt explicitly asks for functional-group counts.

entries.title: Separate electrode equilibrium from kinetic onset and overpotential
entries.use_when: An electrode-reaction problem compares equilibrium, onset, applied potential, overpotential, catalyst activity, or reaction rate across surfaces, conditions, or reference scales.
steps: Assign each potential a physical role and reference scale before comparing values: equilibrium is thermodynamic, whereas onset, current, exchange current, and polarization are kinetic observables.

Under identical reaction conditions and reference scale, derive the equilibrium potential from the redox couple, activities, temperature, and pressure; changing only the catalyst surface changes kinetics, not equilibrium thermodynamics.

Compute signed overpotential as η = E_applied or E_onset - E_eq. For a cathodic process, a more-negative onset gives a lower signed η but a larger positive magnitude |η|, so identify which convention the wording uses.
For proton-coupled couples, align pH and reference electrodes before comparison: a potential may shift with pH versus a fixed reference while remaining invariant versus RHE.
Evaluate every requested descriptor and every clause of a combined choice independently; retain a choice only when its thermodynamic, kinetic, sign-convention, and reference-scale claims all agree.
guards: Do not infer equilibrium potential from observed onset potential or catalyst identity.
Never compare potentials before aligning reference electrodes and thermodynamic conditions.
For cathodic polarization, do not equate a more-negative signed η with a smaller |η|.
One true clause cannot rescue another false clause in a combined statement.

entries.title: Rate ranking from secondary deuterium isotope effects
entries.use_when: Comparing rates of electrophilic addition to isotopologues when the labeled C-H or C-D bonds are not cleaved, especially in rigid or crowded alkenes.
steps: Map every H/D label relative to the reacting center and ask whether its bond is broken in the rate-determining step; if it remains intact, analyze a secondary rather than primary isotope effect.
State the ratio convention: for k_H/k_D, a value below one is inverse and means the deuterated isotopologue is faster.

For electrophilic alkene halogenation, evaluate the transition toward halonium or charge development and changes in coupled C-H/C-D bending and stretching modes; rigid or crowded frameworks can give inverse effects even at homoallylic sites.

Rank isotopologues by the direction and number of comparable contributing labels; combine supported independent site effects multiplicatively, or use only a qualitative cumulative ranking when magnitudes are unavailable.
If the sign for a label class is not established, retrieve a close reaction-class study and preserve uncertainty instead of defaulting to a universal deuterium slowdown.
guards: Do not use the large normal primary isotope-effect rule when no labeled bond is cleaved.
Do not treat remote labels as automatically irrelevant or count all deuteriums without mapping site coupling.
Do not explain inverse effects as literal atomic size alone; use zero-point vibrational and steric-mode changes.
Do not multiply site effects unless equivalence or independence is justified.

entries.title: Nitro-Activated Aromatic Substitution Site Triage
entries.use_when: A strong nucleophile reacts with a nitro-substituted arene containing multiple plausible leaving groups or another base-sensitive linkage.
steps: Atom-map the aromatic ring and list every bond the nucleophile could change, including aryl leaving-group bonds and hydrolysable linkages.
For each aryl leaving group, determine whether a nitro or other strong resonance-withdrawing group is ortho or para; prioritize those sites for classical addition-elimination SNAr.

Treat direct nucleophile-for-halogen replacement at an activated ipso carbon as the canonical SNAr candidate; require independent structural evidence before selecting cleavage elsewhere from reagent identity alone.
Construct the product by replacing only the leaving group at the selected carbon while preserving uninvolved substituents and protected functionality.
Back-map each candidate product and reject denitration, migration, or substitution of hydrogen unless conditions support a separate mechanism.
guards: Do not apply aliphatic SN1/SN2 leaving-group heuristics to aryl halides.
Hydroxide plus heat alone does not identify a sulfonate linkage as the selected reaction site.
Classical SNAr is ipso substitution; preserve the original ring connectivity.
Distinguish an O-sulfonyl protecting group from an arylsulfonyl substituent and state which bond any proposed cleavage breaks.

entries.title: Low-template PCR directional outcome screening
entries.use_when: Use for qualitative PCR or amplification questions that vary starting-template amount and ask for an expected or least-expected outcome.
steps: Parse polarity words such as least, not, and except; restate whether the target is a consistent or inconsistent consequence.
At fixed cycling and reagent conditions, lowering initial template lowers expected product or signal and increases molecule-sampling noise.
Classify dropout, allele or peak imbalance, and weak or failed amplification as low-input-consistent effects; classify increased yield or signal as inconsistent unless compensation is stated.
For a least-expected prompt choose the directionally inconsistent outcome, then recheck the prompt polarity before answering.
guards: Do not select a genuine adverse low-template artifact merely because it is not universal; test causal direction first.
Do not assume compensatory changes such as additional cycles unless stated.
Keep total yield or signal distinct from profile balance and completeness.

entries.title: Reaction-center stereochemical descriptor audit
entries.use_when: A reaction-product choice depends on enolate E/Z geometry or slash/backslash SMILES, especially when changing among ketone, ester, and amide substrates can change both selectivity and CIP interpretation.
steps: Classify the carbonyl derivative and record base, counterion, solvent, temperature, and additives before applying any enolate-geometry trend.

For simple acyclic N,N-disubstituted amides under LDA in THF at low temperature, predict the predominantly Z lithium enolate unless substrate-specific evidence or geometry-altering additives indicate otherwise.
State the predicted same-side or opposite-side substituent relationship independently of the E/Z label.
Assign CIP priorities on each candidate graph and decode directional bonds with atom order and branch placement; use a deterministic stereochemistry parser when available.
Match the verified encoding to the predicted geometry, then emit the requested answer format.
guards: Do not transfer a generic LDA-gives-E heuristic across ketones, esters, and amides.
Slash and backslash are local relative bond directions, not standalone E/Z labels.
Recompute CIP when the carbonyl heteroatom substituent changes; ester and amide enolates can map the same directional pattern differently.
A structure parser validates representation but does not predict reaction selectivity.

entries.title: Heteronuclear and long-range coupling in proton NMR multiplicity
entries.use_when: A proton-NMR multiplicity problem contains fluorine, phosphorus, or another spin-active heteronucleus, especially when a signal appears to lack neighboring protons or the nuclei are connected by a plausible long-range or constrained close-contact pathway.
steps: Assign the likely signal from chemical shift and integration before determining its multiplicity.
Inventory all spin-active coupling partners, not only hydrogens; trace plausible through-bond paths and constrained close contacts that can transmit scalar coupling.
For an ordinary proton spectrum, retain heteronuclear coupling unless decoupling, exchange, or insufficient resolution is stated or strongly implied.
Split sequentially by each inequivalent coupling set: one coupled spin-1/2 nucleus produces a doublet, while additional distinct couplings produce patterns such as doublets of doublets.
Check the proposed multiplicity against coupling-path plausibility, experimental decoupling, and whether the expected J value should be resolved.
guards: Do not apply a proton-only n+1 rule when a coupled spin-active heteronucleus is present.
Do not infer scalar splitting from proximity or an NOE alone; an observable J-coupling mechanism is required.
Do not suppress heteronuclear splitting unless decoupling or non-resolution is supported.
Do not count equivalent protons within the observed group as nuclei that split one another.

entries.title: Atomic spectroscopy model-limit discrimination
entries.use_when: A conceptual atomic-spectroscopy question asks which missing feature of a model explains an observed spectral limitation, especially in multiple-choice form.
steps: Classify the target observable as line position or spacing, line presence or intensity, or another spectral feature.
Map line positions to energy-level accuracy; for multielectron atoms, test whether neglected electron–electron interaction or correlation is the stated limitation.
Map line presence and intensity to transition dipole matrix elements, selection rules, and transition probabilities; quantized levels alone do not supply these.
Compare every supplied choice verbatim, preferring the missing mechanism over its downstream consequence when the prompt asks for the reason or best explanation.
guards: Never replace a choice's wording with a different nearby fact while retaining its label.
Do not confuse energy-level prediction with transition-probability prediction.
Invoke electron–electron interaction only when the target is multielectron energy structure and a supplied choice actually states it.

entries.title: Nucleophile-initiated strained-ring propagation versus quenched addition
entries.use_when: A qualitative reactivity or compatibility question pairs a nucleophile or base with an epoxide or another strained heterocyclic monomer and asks whether the outcome is initiation, propagation, or an isolated ring-opened product.
steps: Classify the context before naming a product: distinguish a single-substrate synthesis with explicit quench or workup from a monomer, bulk-mixture, compatibility, or hazard setting.
Draw the first elementary step and retain its charge: nucleophilic ring opening normally gives an anionic heteroatom terminus, not a neutral product unless a proton source is supplied.

When more strained-ring monomer is available and no terminating proton source is stated, test one propagation step in which the anionic terminus attacks another monomer; classify the original reagent as an initiator if chain growth is viable.

Choose a discrete ring-opened addition product only when stoichiometry and an explicit proton donor, quench, or workup terminate the active center; when conditions are underspecified, use the question framing and option semantics to distinguish synthetic-product from compatibility intent.
guards: Do not invent protonation, hydrolysis, or workup conditions that the prompt does not supply.
Do not stop at the first ring-opened intermediate before testing whether its charged terminus can attack another monomer.
Do not claim polymerization for every nucleophile-ring pair; require a polymerizable strained monomer, a viable propagating center, and no dominant termination condition.

entries.title: Diazonium salt isolation and temperature-role safety
entries.use_when: A diazonium-safety or synthesis question asks for a temperature limit, especially when preparation, operation, handling, and decomposition temperatures could be confused.
steps: Classify every temperature by physical role: preparation setpoint, reaction temperature, generic handling or heating ceiling, or compound-specific decomposition onset.
For maximum or should-not-exceed wording, retrieve authoritative safety guidance using ceiling or heating terminology; do not substitute a classroom preparation temperature.
Match the supported temperature role to the requested role before comparing options; a smaller value is not automatically the answer to an exact-ceiling question.
Treat generic guidance as a screening bound only because counterion, concentration, impurities, physical state, and thermal characterization can require stricter controls.
guards: Never infer an exact ceiling from qualitative instability or low-temperature synthesis conditions.
If no authoritative source supports the requested temperature role, report insufficient support rather than guessing.
Do not present a generic ceiling as a safe operating target or guarantee.
Compound-specific thermal testing and institutional procedures supersede generic guidance.

entries.title: Explosive performance metric role disambiguation
entries.use_when: A conceptual energetic-materials task asks which quantities characterize general detonation performance or contrasts detonation-front, thermochemical, and metal-acceleration metrics.
steps: Identify whether the requested scope is general detonation characterization, safety or sensitivity, or a specific application such as accelerating a casing or fragments.
Classify each candidate quantity by physical role: propagation, detonation-state pressure, thermochemical energy release, or expansion-driven metal acceleration.

For broad characterization, require coverage of propagation, pressure or shock intensity, and energy release; elevate a Gurney-type metric when the prompt specifically concerns casing, fragments, cylinder expansion, or delivered mechanical work.
Compare choices by role coverage and reject a set that replaces thermochemical energy with an application-specific acceleration surrogate under a general scope.
guards: Do not treat a metric as core merely because it is widely reported.
Keep detonation performance distinct from sensitivity, thermal stability, and handling safety unless requested.
Preserve distinctions among heat of explosion, heat of detonation, heat of formation, and heat of combustion.
Account for loading density, confinement, and test definition when comparing measured values.

entries.title: Qualitative ionic solubility and aqueous causticity screening
entries.use_when: Comparing ionic compounds by aqueous solubility, corrosivity, or causticity, especially salts containing a strongly basic anion such as sulfide.
steps: Parse each salt into its cation and anion; distinguish sulfide from sulfate before applying any rule.
Apply high-priority cation rules first: Group 1 and ammonium salts are generally water-soluble.
For remaining sulfides, recognize that most transition- and heavy-metal sulfides are insoluble; when uncertainty matters, search for and call the ionic-solubility predictor on each candidate.
Connect solubility to causticity: dissolved sulfide hydrolyzes water to form hydrosulfide and hydroxide, whereas limited dissolution suppresses this aqueous basicity.
Select by the property actually requested, keeping corrosivity, solubility, and toxicity separate.
guards: Do not classify every sulfide as insoluble before checking soluble-cation exceptions.
Do not confuse sulfide with sulfate or apply sulfate exceptions.
Do not equate low causticity or low solubility with low toxicity.
Treat rule-based predictions as screening guidance when pH, complexation, or measured solubility could change the result.

entries.title: Purification feasibility by speciation, phase, and unit-operation audit
entries.use_when: A purification or separation claim depends on whether reagents cause redox, complexation, dissolution, precipitation, or transfer between phases.
steps: List target and impurity species before and after each stated condition, including phases and oxidation states.
Classify each transformation independently as redox, acid-base reaction, complexation, dissolution or leaching, precipitation, or phase transfer.
Build an operation ledger distinguishing reaction, leaching, liquid-liquid extraction, evaporation, and filtration; count only operations stated or required by phase evidence.
Track target, impurity, and byproducts through every phase and verify that the stated recovery operation actually separates them.
Evaluate every claim independently, preserve separately verified quantitative conclusions, and map the complete truth set only at the end.
guards: An oxidizing or reducing medium does not prove that every dissolved species changes oxidation state.
Halide formation or complexation is not redox unless the central atom's oxidation state changes.
Do not infer liquid-liquid extraction from dissolution, leaching, precipitation, or filtration.
A chemical transformation alone does not prove purification without a valid phase-separation and recovery step.

entries.title: Water-assisted N-aryl ketonitrone–alkyne cascade mapping
entries.use_when: An N-aryl alpha,beta-unsaturated ketonitrone reacts with an electron-poor alkyne and candidate products share global formula or ring-count constraints but differ in connectivity after a water-assisted seven-membered intermediate.
steps: Label the nitrone carbon and oxygen, conjugated alpha/beta carbons, N-aryl ipso and ortho atoms, and both alkyne carbons and substituents; maintain a bond-change and atom-fate table.
Test stepwise oxygen addition, formal [5+2] closure, and nitrone C=N geometry adjustment leading to a seven-membered intermediate instead of defaulting to an ordinary [3+2] cycloadduct.

When trace or catalytic water is stated, place hydrolysis of the cyclic iminium/acetal-like intermediate before or adjacent to the [3,3] rearrangement; require the resulting carbonyl-bearing open-chain connectivity and regeneration of water during condensation.

Carry the [3,3] rearrangement, tautomerization, and intramolecular condensation to completion; verify a C3-quaternary indolenine by an explicit fused five-membered ring containing C=N and a quaternary C3, distinguishing it from an NH indoline.

Filter candidate structures by formula and ring count, then compare exact nitrone-derived carbonyl-tether connectivity and placement of the activated-alkyne substituents; settle connectivity before stereochemistry.
guards: Do not assign an indolenine label from visual resemblance; explicitly locate the ring C=N bond and quaternary C3.
Matching molecular formula and total ring count cannot distinguish constitutional isomers.
Do not treat a trace-water cue as generic proton transfer when the proposed cascade contains a hydrolysis step.
Do not use stereochemical wedges as tie-breakers until constitution and functional-group placement agree.

entries.title: Organic nitro-subclass oxidizer and hazard comparison
entries.use_when: A question compares oxidizing strength or incompatibility hazards among organic nitro subclasses, especially simple nitroalkanes and nitroaromatic compounds.
steps: Identify the requested property as oxidizer or compatibility behavior; do not substitute acidity, nitronate formation, synthetic reactivity, or electrophilic-substitution behavior.
Classify each compound as a nitroalkane, nitroaromatic, nitrate or nitrite ester, or multiply nitrated material before comparing it.
For reactive-group comparisons of simple nitroalkanes with nitroaromatics, treat nitroalkanes as the milder oxidizing subclass.
Keep milder distinct from inert: nitroalkanes can still react violently with reducing agents at elevated temperature or pressure and can form hazardous salts with bases.
Translate the supported qualitative relation into the visible answer wording only after the chemical comparison is fixed.
guards: Do not infer oxidizer strength solely from the nitrogen oxidation state or the presence of a nitro group.
Do not use alpha-hydrogen acidity or nitronate chemistry to reverse an oxidizer-strength comparison.
Do not equate milder with nonreactive.
Do not extrapolate the simple-subclass ordering to nitrate esters or multiply nitrated energetic materials without compound-specific evidence.

entries.title: Early virtual-screening whole-profile comparison
entries.use_when: Comparing molecular structures using generic oral-availability, drug-likeness, or small-molecule profile cues without target-specific potency data.
steps: Build the same side-by-side profile for every candidate: molecular weight, cLogP, polar surface area, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, rotatable bonds, ring and aromatic burden, fraction sp3, and ionizable groups; for valid SMILES, prefer a parser-backed descriptor calculation.

Before trusting calculated descriptors, confirm that every SMILES parsed and produced plausible nonzero values; otherwise make an explicit structural-proxy table using atom and halogen burden, rings, heteroatoms, flexibility, and ionization.

Use Lipinski and Veber as coarse screens, then compare continuous margins and a consistently computed composite drug-likeness measure or whole-profile balance; treat several large adverse margins as material.
Separate solubility and salt-forming potential from permeability and exposure, then choose only after identifying which candidate wins each major dimension and any decisive liabilities.
Emit the requested leading option token followed by a concise rationale tied to the profile differences.
guards: Do not let one favorable group or one binary threshold dominate several adverse continuous margins.
Do not accept zero or default descriptors from a tool that did not parse the supplied SMILES.
Use identical descriptor methods and protonation conventions across candidates.
Do not infer potency, safety, or clinical bioavailability from generic drug-likeness descriptors.

entries.title: Exact-scope verification of chemical application claims
entries.use_when: A qualitative or multi-select chemistry question asks whether a named substance is used for a stated process, target, commodity, facility, or purpose, especially when historical and current uses may differ.
steps: Decompose each use claim into substance or formulation, function, target or commodity, venue, and time or jurisdiction.
Search the exact function-target pair, separating current registration or practice from historical use and prioritizing authoritative regulatory or technical sources.
Accept a claim only when the evidence matches its target, venue, and temporal wording; a broad use category or adjacent commodity does not entail the narrower statement.
Resolve apparent conflicts by distinguishing current, permitted, historical, and discontinued uses, then evaluate every option independently.
Return all selected option letters in the requested order and format before any explanation.
guards: A generic fumigant or sterilant label does not prove a specific application.
Historical use does not establish current use, and current nonuse does not establish that a substance was never used.
Do not interchange similar chemical names, mixtures, or formulations.
Empty retrieval is not supporting evidence; do not strengthen an unsupported recollection into a specific claim.

entries.title: Phase-aware release hazard and response selection
entries.use_when: A qualitative chemical-safety question asks for the most direct hazard or applicable response associated with gas or vapor accumulation, especially in a confined or poorly ventilated space.
steps: Determine whether the stem asks about an intrinsic substance property or a hazard created by the stated phase, accumulation, ventilation, and surroundings.
Map the visible choices to mechanisms such as oxygen depletion, dose-dependent poisoning, ignition, corrosive contact, or sensory nuisance.

Rank choices by direct support from the stated scenario: confined gas accumulation supports an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, while toxicity, ignition, or corrosion require corresponding substance-specific or situational evidence.
Select the single most directly entailed category rather than every plausible secondary hazard, then preserve the requested answer format.
guards: Do not let a merely plausible intrinsic toxicity override the mechanism explicitly established by the scenario.
Do not classify every confined-space gas as a simple oxygen displacer when the stem supplies specific toxicant, oxygen-reactive, or ignition evidence.
Do not promote odor, corrosion, or another secondary property without the exposure pathway or contact condition that makes it directly relevant.

entries.title: Equilibrium-Limited Catalytic Conversion Triage
entries.use_when: A reversible catalytic reaction gives the same outlet composition after catalyst loading or catalyst-composition changes, and proposed remedies use temperature or catalyst changes to raise per-pass conversion.
steps: Treat an invariant outlet composition despite adequate activity and catalyst changes as evidence for an equilibrium plateau, while checking whether stated residence-time or transport limitations contradict that diagnosis.
Separate kinetics from thermodynamics: a catalyst can accelerate equilibration and alter selectivity but cannot change the equilibrium constant at fixed thermodynamic conditions.
Balance the reaction and assess actual equilibrium levers using reaction-enthalpy sign and magnitude, gas-mole change, feed activities, pressure, and product removal.
Apply a van't Hoff magnitude check; for nearly thermoneutral bond-exchange reactions, modest temperature changes cannot be assumed to produce a meaningful equilibrium shift.

Compare the attainable shift with the requested magnitude and constraints; if no proposed lever can materially move equilibrium, accept the per-pass plateau or consider separation and recycle rather than more catalyst.
guards: Do not infer that a reaction is exothermic or endothermic from its name or catalyst behavior.
Do not claim that more catalyst changes equilibrium conversion.
Do not confuse a favorable shift direction with a substantial change; magnitude-check the equilibrium constant.
Do not recommend temperature changes without considering their effects on rate, selectivity, and side reactions.

entries.title: Condition-coupled spin, electron-configuration, and exact-geometry audit
entries.use_when: A coordination or organometallic problem couples electron-count rules, magnetic state, valence-orbital occupation, or an exact geometry claim across pressure, temperature, or another ligand-field perturbation.
steps: Build a condition-by-condition table separating total valence electrons or EAN, metal-centered configuration, unpaired-electron count, coordination number, and exact geometry or symmetry.
Count electrons independently of geometry; unchanged composition can preserve total electron count while pressure or ligand-field changes redistribute electrons between ns and d orbitals.

For each proposed geometry, fill its symmetry-specific orbital levels and compare the predicted spin. For high-spin tetrahedral d6, e3t2^3 gives four unpaired electrons but an orbitally degenerate, distortion-prone state, so regular Td requires direct support.

For four-coordinate species, compare tetrahedral, distorted or seesaw, and square-planar candidates; when spin or orbital occupation changes, test both geometry-preserving and geometry-changing models against structural, spectroscopic, or theoretical evidence.
Evaluate every statement independently, then map the exact truth set to the requested answer representation.
guards: Do not use EAN or the 18-electron rule as a geometry proof.
Do not equate coordination number four or high spin with a regular tetrahedron.
Do not transfer octahedral spin tables unchanged to tetrahedral, square-planar, or low-symmetry structures.
Do not infer an exact point group from diamagnetism alone.

entries.title: Coupled real-gas equilibrium and ideal-model error analysis
entries.use_when: Use when an equilibrium composition, remaining phase, or reaction extent at fixed total pressure must be compared between ideal-gas and componentwise van der Waals models, especially when inert gases are present.
steps: Form the standard reaction enthalpy and entropy, compute the standard Gibbs energy at the stated temperature, and obtain the dimensionless equilibrium constant; omit a pure condensed phase only while it remains present.

Parameterize every amount by reaction extent and common volume. For a stated separate-component van der Waals convention, set c_i=n_i/V, compute p_i=RTc_i/(1-b_i c_i)-a_i c_i^2, and enforce the total-pressure sum.

Enforce the dimensionless equilibrium relation using component pressures, or fugacities only when explicitly required, and solve jointly for extent and volume on the feasible branch; repeat with a_i=b_i=0 for the ideal comparison.
Convert both solutions to the requested mass, volume, or extent and compare their absolute difference before classifying its order of magnitude.
Check the correction scale with B_i=b_i-a_i/(RT) and Z_i-1 approximately B_i p_i/(RT); investigate any extent shift much larger than the underlying EOS deviations.
guards: Include inert species in pressure and volume closure even though they are absent from the reaction quotient.
Do not substitute total pressure for component pressure or silently introduce fugacity and mixture rules beyond the stated model.
Keep pressure activities dimensionless and use one consistent unit system for R, a, b, pressure, and volume.
Require positive free volumes and inventory-bounded extents; if a condensed reactant is exhausted, switch to the appropriate phase regime.

entries.title: Competitive ITC affinity identifiability
entries.use_when: An ITC displacement or competition problem asks for an intrinsic binding constant from a fitted affinity measured in the presence of another ligand.
steps: Label every reported constant by experiment and fit model: intrinsic single-ligand constant, conditional apparent constant, or parameter from a competitive global fit.
Require mutually exclusive binding at the same independent sites; shared inhibition and near-unity stoichiometry alone do not establish competition.
Only for a fixed-free-competitor one-site model use Kd,app,A = Kd,A(1 + [B]free/Kd,B), equivalently Ka,A = (1 + [B]free/Kd,B)/Kd,app,A.
Derive free competitor by mass balance rather than using nominal excess; if concentrations change during injections, use the full conservation and heat model.
If the binding model, free-concentration trajectory, or fitted-parameter meaning is unspecified, report the intrinsic affinity as non-identifiable instead of forcing a numerical conversion.
guards: Do not infer a shared binding site merely because both ligands bind one target with similar stoichiometry.
Do not assume a displacement-run fitted Kd is an apparent or intrinsic Kd without the stated fitting model.
Do not substitute total competitor for free competitor when binding depletion can be material.
Do not add a deterministic calculator when missing model assumptions, rather than arithmetic, prevent a unique result.

entries.title: Natural toxin process-fate and mechanism audit
entries.use_when: A qualitative or multi-select toxicology question asks whether a natural protein toxin remains in a processed oil, is inactivated during processing, or acts through a proposed cellular target.
steps: Classify the toxin chemically: water-soluble proteins generally follow aqueous or solid residue rather than a neutral lipid fraction.
Trace pressing, phase separation, refining, heating, and waste streams separately; product absence may reflect partitioning, removal, thermal inactivation, or several mechanisms.
Evaluate thermal claims against process conditions: sufficiently hot and long treatment can denature protein toxins, whereas cold pressing alone does not establish inactivation.
Check the molecular target independently: ribosome-inactivating proteins enzymatically damage rRNA and halt protein synthesis rather than primarily disrupting ion channels.
Match every statement to conventional versus explicitly cold processing, evaluate selections independently, and return the complete requested set.
guards: Do not infer destruction solely from absence in a product; distinguish phase partitioning, physical removal, and inactivation.
Do not apply heated-process conclusions to explicitly cold processing.
For conventional commercial processing, do not reject an authoritative heat-inactivation claim merely because phase partitioning is also operative.
Do not confuse a protein toxin with lipid-derived constituents from the same biological source.

entries.title: Unit-cell density and composition constraint triangulation
entries.use_when: A crystalline coordination compound or porous framework identity must be inferred from cell parameters, density, Z, elemental ratios, included solvent or guests, and a decomposition-product composition.
steps: Convert lattice lengths to a consistent unit, obtain the crystal-system cell volume, and infer formula-unit molar mass from M = rho*V*N_A/Z with V in cm^3.
Construct complete charge-balanced candidate formula units from linker, guest, and elemental-ratio evidence; include coordinated or occluded solvent when its elements are observed.
Round-trip each candidate with the framework-density calculation and compare discrepancies against the precision of the crystallographic measurements.
Calculate metal fractions for chemically plausible oxidation products, treating rounded percentages as corroborating tolerance bands rather than unique identifiers.
Select the identity satisfying all independent constraints, then map it to the requested answer format.
guards: Treat Z as formula units per cell, not an atom count.
Convert cubic angstroms to cubic centimeters with 1e-24, or convert picometers before calculating volume.
Do not omit solvent or guest mass when elemental evidence includes its atoms.
Do not let one rounded oxide percentage override a precise cell-density and formula-mass match.

entries.title: Fractional-coordinate polyhedron metric reconstruction
entries.use_when: A crystal-structure problem gives fractional coordinates or layered symmetry, a distorted-polyhedron angle, and asks for a lattice parameter or local geometry.
steps: Enumerate the symmetry-related and periodic-image vertices that actually form the stated polyhedron, using nearest-image fractional differences.
Convert every fractional difference with the lattice matrix. For tetragonal vertices (±a/2,0,zc) and (0,±a/2,(1-z)c), define Δ=|1-2z|c and construct the edge vectors explicitly.
Compute all unique angle classes from cos θ=(u·v)/(|u||v|). For this disphenoid, the classes obey cos θ1=a/[2√(a²/2+Δ²)] and cos θ2=Δ²/(a²/2+Δ²).
Match the stated larger or smaller angle before solving. For the θ2 class, use c=a√[cos θ/(2(1-cos θ))]/|1-2z|; otherwise solve the corresponding dot-product equation.
Back-substitute the result to reproduce every angle class and check periodic images, units, and option rounding.
guards: Never treat one fractional-axis component as a complete Cartesian edge length.
Do not choose an angle equation until all unique angle classes have been calculated and ordered.
Apply symmetry and minimum-image conventions before computing distances or angles.
Reject a solution that fails back-substitution into the reported angle class.

entries.title: Heme toxicant target and oxidation-state scope
entries.use_when: A qualitative chemistry or toxicology question compares ligand binding, oxidation, denaturation, or no interaction across hemoglobin states and other hemoprotein targets.
steps: Separate the prompt’s exact target claim from the substance’s dominant whole-body toxicity mechanism.
Distinguish functional ferrous hemoglobin, ferric methemoglobin, and ferric heme centers in respiratory enzymes before judging binding or redox claims.
For cyanide, recognize coordination to ferric heme: it binds methemoglobin and inhibits cytochrome oxidase, while binding normal ferrous hemoglobin poorly; binding is not denaturation or oxidation.
Evaluate each visible option at its stated scope: reject an absolute no-interaction claim when a documented heme-state interaction exists, then choose the least overbroad true statement.
Return the requested option format before explanation.
guards: Do not use the dominant toxic target to negate a real secondary blood interaction.
Do not collapse functional hemoglobin and methemoglobin into the same iron oxidation state.
Do not equate ligand binding with oxidation, denaturation, or the primary cause of toxicity.
Do not add a deterministic tool for a qualitative reference-fact distinction.

entries.title: Direction-aware empirical activation-energy estimation
entries.use_when: An empirical activation-energy rule is qualified by reaction direction or exothermicity, especially when the requested elementary radical step is endothermic but its reverse is exothermic.
steps: Inventory bonds broken and formed in the requested direction, then estimate ΔHforward as the sum of broken-bond energies minus the sum of formed-bond energies.
Apply a direction-qualified empirical coefficient only when that direction satisfies its stated condition; otherwise examine the reverse reaction.
For an endothermic target whose reverse is covered, calculate Ea,reverse from bonds broken in reverse, then use Ea,forward = Ea,reverse + ΔHforward.
Compare unrounded estimates with experimental values, verify difference and relative-error signs, and round only the final reported comparison.
guards: Never apply an exothermic-step coefficient directly to an endothermic target direction.
Require Ea,forward − Ea,reverse to equal ΔHforward with the same sign.
Remember that bonds broken in reverse are bonds formed forward.
If no direction satisfies a rule's stated category, do not force that coefficient.

entries.title: Verify reaction-based assay applicability before transferring stoichiometry
entries.use_when: A titrimetric or derivatization assay asks whether a structurally related analyte can be measured by the same reaction and conditions.
steps: Identify the analytical reaction, measured reagent equivalents, medium, reaction time, and proposed product for each analyte independently.
Require rapid and near-complete conversion, adequate selectivity, and a reproducible fixed reagent-to-analyte stoichiometry; mere qualitative reaction feasibility is insufficient.

For phenolic iodination, map free ring hydrogens and hydroxyl activation, then verify substitution extent: highly activated polyhydroxy rings may undergo exhaustive substitution, whereas monohydric phenol can give condition-dependent mono-, di-, and tri-substituted mixtures.
Only after assay applicability is established should its equivalent factor enter the back-titration balance; evaluate qualitative scope claims separately from otherwise correct arithmetic.
guards: Qualitative reactivity does not establish quantitative assayability.
