Do not transfer stoichiometric equivalents between analogs without product-distribution evidence.
Do not let correct titration arithmetic validate a separate method-scope claim.
Do not generalize pH, time, or substitution extent across phenolic substrates.

entries.title: Coordination-complex composition, topology, and stereochemical symmetry audit
entries.use_when: A mono- or polynuclear coordination-complex problem asks about composition or reaction balance, donor geometry or orbital types, chelate-ring sizes, local Δ/Λ configurations, metal-site equivalence, molecular symmetry, or stability claims.
steps: Build the full coordination graph, including ligand formal charges and denticity, released ligands and protons, and counterions; balance atoms and charge before comparing coefficient sums.

For each metal, list donor atoms, coordination number, geometry, and oxidation or d-electron count; if hybridization language is requested, count angular-momentum orbital types rather than individual orbitals.
Enumerate independent organic cycles and metallacycles and record the atom count of each; distinguish ring size from ring identity and follow the stated counting scope before collapsing categories.

Assign local Δ/Λ descriptors, then test site equivalence using a full-structure symmetry operation that maps one metal and every labeled donor path onto the other; proper operations preserve local handedness, whereas inversion or reflection reverses it.
Toggle every stereogenic element that the question includes or excludes, audit each statement independently, and only then map the true-statement set to the visible choices.
guards: Identical local Δ/Λ labels do not prove metal-site equivalence; require a valid full-molecule symmetry mapping.
A heterochiral descriptor pair does not by itself prove centrosymmetry or exceptional stability; the bridge, donor labels, conformation, and all included stereogenic centers must also map.
Do not conflate chelate-ring size, aromatic-ring size, and connectivity when counting ring types; state the counting convention.
Reject an atom-balanced synthesis if charge, protons, displaced ligands, or counterions are inconsistent.

entries.title: Peroxo-crystal speciation and TGA closure
entries.use_when: A crystalline inorganic peroxide or peroxosalt identity, component ratio, or statement set must be inferred from preparation, ionic and neutral species, and thermogravimetric mass loss.
steps: Write charged and neutral crystal components separately; distinguish hydrogen-monoperoxocarbonate such as HCO4-, peroxodicarbonate C2O6^2-, and neutral H2O2 of crystallization before collapsing to an empirical formula.

Check whether constitutional candidates share aggregate atom counts on a common formula-unit basis; if they do, TGA cannot determine their ion and guest multiplicities, so use preparation and crystallographic identity evidence for speciation.
For each viable constitution, compute the retained-residue fraction on a stoichiometrically matched basis and reject candidates inconsistent with the measured mass loss.

Balance all solid and volatile products with coprime coefficients, then derive component ratios and reaction coefficients from the accepted constitutional formula rather than its empirical composition.
Evaluate symmetry and bond-length claims independently from the actual conformation or reliable structural data before combining statement results and mapping the requested answer format.
guards: One type of cation, anion, or neutral species states chemical identity, not stoichiometric count.
Elemental and TGA agreement does not prove constitutional speciation when candidates are isocompositional.
Do not infer symmetry elements or peroxo-bond ordering from the word peroxide alone.
Match formula-unit and residue coefficients before comparing molar masses.

entries.title: Matched acid and counteranion trend audit
entries.use_when: A matched substituent series compares both Brønsted acidity and coordination or ion-pairing of the corresponding conjugate anions, especially with highly electrophilic cations and weakly coordinating cluster anions.
steps: Write the neutral-acid and conjugate-anion series separately, and identify which property each claim ranks.
Rank acid strength through conjugate-base stabilization or proton affinity: a stronger acid has a less basic conjugate anion.
For the same cation under comparable conditions, infer direct anion coordination oppositely to acid strength, then account for substituent polarizability, softness, sterics, and charge exposure.
Cross-check interaction strength with association energies, cation distortion, vibrational shifts, or other direct observables before completing the statement truth set.
guards: Never copy an acidity order directly onto conjugate-anion coordination without inversion and an interaction-specific check.
Do not compare raw contact distances across different atom sizes as a standalone measure of interaction strength.
Do not assume a weakly coordinating anion is noninteracting with a highly electrophilic cation.
Do not transfer solid-state or solvent-specific ion-pair trends across unmatched conditions.

entries.title: F-block scorpionate condition and coordination audit
entries.use_when: An f-block coordination problem combines an element-identification clue, a poly(pyrazolyl)borate reagent, reaction conditions, and a requested metal, oxidation state, ligand set, or coordination number.
steps: Enumerate element candidates from every naming and physical-property clue; for density anomalies record allotrope, temperature, pressure, and source precision before excluding candidates.
Preserve the precursor metal and oxidation state unless an explicit redox or transmetalation step changes them, then build a ligand charge and donor-count ledger.

Treat hydrotris(pyrazolyl)borate as monoanionic and usually tridentate; under dry crowded f-block coordination, B-N cleavage can supply a bidentate azolate, while oxo-boroxane products require a credible water or oxygen source.
Expand omitted ligand multiplicities and verify coordination number by summing multiplicity times denticity; use charge neutrality as an independent check.
Select a catch-all choice only after every explicit composition has failed the identity, condition, charge, and coordination audits.
guards: Astronomical naming is not a unique element identifier; reconcile it with the full constraint set.
Do not infer an unlisted metal from one clue and stop before auditing the synthetic evidence.
Count donor atoms, not ligand names; multiplicity and binding mode are part of the formula.
Do not invoke a hydrolysis-derived ligand under explicitly dry conditions without a stated oxygen source.

entries.title: Mercury toxicology by species, latency, and endpoint type
entries.use_when: A mercury toxicology question asks which clinical effect best matches an exposure form, route, duration, latency, or endpoint type.
steps: Classify mercury form, exposure route, duration, latency, and population from the stem and options.
Separate patient symptoms and adverse effects from examination signs, exposure biomarkers, renal findings, and acute local injury.

Map organic mercury primarily to delayed sensory and cerebellar central-nervous-system toxicity; map chronic elemental or inorganic exposure to tremor, behavioral change, oral inflammation, and renal effects; map ingested inorganic salts to acute corrosive and renal injury.
Rank candidates using the complete exposure pattern and requested endpoint type, then return only the requested answer representation.
guards: Do not treat a memorable eponym as the key symptom without checking whether it is only an exposure marker.
Mercurialentis is lens-capsule discoloration rather than lens opacity and can occur as an exposure biomarker without adverse ocular effects.
When mercury species is unstated, infer it only from the joint latency, route, organ-system, and option clues.

entries.title: Vibrational partition-function convention and approximation thresholds
entries.use_when: Comparing exact and high-temperature harmonic-oscillator vibrational partition functions or finding a temperature at which their percentage difference reaches a tolerance.
steps: Set the characteristic temperature theta = hc times wavenumber divided by k and define x = theta/T.

Match the energy-zero convention to the stated approximation: with the vibrational ground level as zero, use q_exact = 1/(1-exp(-x)) and q_HT = 1/x; include the exp(-x/2) factor only when zero-point energy is explicitly retained.
Write the fractional-error denominator explicitly. Unless another reference is specified, test the approximation against the exact value using abs(q_HT-q_exact)/q_exact.
Solve the dimensionless boundary error(x)=p for positive x, compute T_threshold=theta/x, and verify that increasing temperature decreases the error.
Use the small-x checks error approximately x/2 for the excitation-zero convention and approximately x^2/24 for the zero-point-energy-including convention to detect a convention mismatch.
guards: Do not mix partition functions with different energy-zero conventions.
Do not leave the percentage-error denominator implicit.
Distinguish the minimum threshold temperature from an arbitrary temperature satisfying the tolerance.
Treat a numerical root as valid only after checking the high-temperature limit and monotonic direction.

entries.title: Separate conformational access from conditional binding stabilization
entries.use_when: A medicinal-chemistry comparison asks how cyclization or scaffold rigidity affects conformational access, productive recognition, affinity, selectivity, or interaction strength, especially in a negative-polarity multiple-choice task.
steps: Lock the requested polarity before judging the choices, and restate whether the task seeks the true or false claim.
Separate free-ligand conformational access from conditional stabilization of a bound complex; these are different stages and can change in different directions.

Treat rigidity as narrowing the accessible ensemble. Infer better binding only when that ensemble is known to include a target-compatible bioactive geometry; otherwise rigidity can reduce the chance of reaching one.
Truth-value every choice under the same comparison scope, reject unconditional causal overclaims, and emit the requested answer token with a concise rationale.
guards: Do not infer target complementarity from rigidity or cyclization alone.
Do not equate fewer conformations with automatically favorable binding entropy or affinity; geometry, strain, enthalpy, and solvation can offset it.
For negative-polarity questions, independently audit every choice before selecting one.

entries.title: Compound-specific toxicity within broad chemical classes
entries.use_when: A qualitative toxicology question compares broad chemical families or asks whether every member of a class shares one toxicity level.
steps: Identify the classification level of each claim: exact compound, narrow homologous series, functional subclass, or broad chemical family.
At broad-family level, audit whether structure, substitution, oxidation state or speciation, physical properties, dose, and exposure route can materially change toxicokinetics or toxicodynamics.

Reject a universal class ranking unless the question supplies a restricted scope or reliable evidence that supports it; a memorable hazardous member is not representative evidence for the whole family.
Evaluate each answer choice at the same stated level of generality, distinguishing intrinsic hazard from exposure-dependent risk, before selecting the best-supported claim.
guards: A shared functional-group label does not imply uniform toxicity.
Do not infer a family-wide hazard from one well-known toxic member.
Keep intrinsic toxicity separate from exposure probability and risk.
Empty retrieval is not evidence for a remembered class-wide rule; preserve uncertainty instead.

entries.title: Atom-scaled redox half-reaction electron ledger
entries.use_when: A half-reaction must be balanced in acidic or basic medium, especially when a polyatomic reactant forms a molecular product containing multiple atoms of the redox-active element.
steps: First balance the redox-active element, including any factor required by a diatomic or polyatomic product; do not calculate electrons on an unscaled skeleton.

For a one-reactant to one-product half-reaction, call equation_balancing_tools.balance_redox_half_reaction with formulas, charges, and medium; require its structured atom and charge audit to report balanced before using the electron count.
Balance oxygen with water and hydrogen with hydrogen ion in acidic medium; for basic medium, complete the acidic form first and then neutralize hydrogen ion with hydroxide.
Place electrons on the side that makes total charge equal, and independently verify the count as oxidation-state change per atom multiplied by the number of transformed atoms.
Recount every element and net charge on both sides, reduce to the smallest valid integer coefficients, and only then map electron side and count to an answer choice.
guards: Multiply a per-atom oxidation-number change by every transformed atom in the balanced skeleton.
Electrons appear on the reactant side for a reduction and on the product side for an oxidation.
Never infer the electron count before balancing the redox-active element.
A valid half-reaction must conserve both atoms and net charge.

entries.title: Temperature-shifted carbonate alkalinity and scale limits
entries.use_when: A water-scaling or hardness problem changes temperature and couples gas-buffered carbonate speciation to saturation of more than one calcium, magnesium, carbonate, or hydroxide solid.
steps: From the stated formation enthalpies and entropies, form each required reaction and compute its equilibrium constant at the target temperature from reaction Gibbs energy; keep the reaction direction explicit.

Use the initial pH, gas partial pressure, and carbonate equilibria to establish the conserved analytical alkalinity or other conserved inventory before heating rather than carrying the initial pH forward.

At the target temperature and stated gas boundary condition, solve charge or alkalinity balance together with carbonate acid-base equilibria to obtain free hydroxide, bicarbonate, and carbonate concentrations.

Apply each candidate solid's solubility product independently to the target free-ion concentrations, sum the allowed dissolved metal concentrations requested by the problem, and convert the total once to the specified hardness basis.
Check reaction signs, concentration units, omitted scale formers, and whether the gas boundary is open or closed before comparing with numerical choices.
guards: Do not hold pH fixed across a temperature change unless the problem explicitly imposes it.
Distinguish conserved alkalinity from temperature-dependent species concentrations.
Use free-ion activities or stated concentration approximations in each solubility product.
Include every independently limiting scale former before converting the summed hardness.

entries.title: Constraint-first inorganic reaction and coefficient audit
entries.use_when: An inorganic reaction or multi-process equation-selection problem requires product identification, balancing, coefficient-derived statements, or enforcement of verbal constraints such as phase, product count, compound type, or the identity and number of gases.
steps: Translate every verbal condition into a pre-balance constraint ledger, including phases, product count and type, oxidation environment, and allowed gas classes; normalize translated language so one simple gaseous substance means exactly one elemental gas, then call reaction_constraint_tools.audit_gas_product_constraints and require accepted=true.

Interpret a stated 1:1 ionic compound as one cation unit per anion unit. For a group-4 oxo cation MO2+ with sulfate, use the 1:1 oxosulfate MOSO4 rather than the 1:2 normal sulfate M(SO4)2; when this is coupled to acid-protonated nitride and one elemental gas, derive and atom-audit the constrained family before computing coefficients.

Propose products consistent with every constraint, reject any equation that introduces a forbidden extra product even if its atoms can be balanced, then balance atoms and charge, reduce to the smallest whole-number vector, and label reactant-side, product-side, and full-equation coefficient sets.
For each process, compute every requested sum, difference, product, ratio, primality, or coefficient occurrence from that normalized ledger without carrying values between processes.
Evaluate every statement independently against the same constraint and coefficient ledgers, then check option-set uniqueness before selecting a single-best or catch-all response.
guards: Atom balance alone does not validate product identities or satisfy verbal product constraints.
An equation that releases two gases cannot satisfy a one-gas condition, and an elemental-gas constraint rejects compound gases such as SO2 even when only one gas formula appears.
A stated 1:1 ionic product rejects a normal 1:2 sulfate when the chemistry instead specifies a divalent oxo cation paired with sulfate.
Normalize coefficients before computing any aggregate, and do not infer one process statement from another process's equation or coefficient ledger.

entries.title: Exact finite rectangular-barrier transmission
entries.use_when: A particle-transmission calculation specifies a finite rectangular barrier, especially when the barrier is thin, the particle energy is near the barrier height, or the expected transmission is not very small.
steps: For E < V0, convert mass, energy, and width consistently, then compute kappa = sqrt(2m(V0-E))/hbar and z = kappa*a.
Use the interface-matched result T = [1 + V0^2*sinh^2(z)/(4E(V0-E))]^-1. For repeatable numerics, search for and call tunneling_calculator.transmission_rectangular_exact with SI inputs.

Use exp(-2z) only as a leading WKB estimate when z is much greater than 1 or an approximation is explicitly requested; the thick-barrier finite-step asymptotic also contains the prefactor 16E(V0-E)/V0^2.
Check that 0 <= T <= 1 and that T approaches 1 as the width approaches zero; report the dimensionless probability rather than a percentage unless requested.
guards: Do not use a default mass near 1 amu for an electron; bind the actual particle mass.
Do not treat z near or below unity as a thick-barrier WKB regime.
Do not apply the below-barrier sinh expression at or above the barrier height; use the appropriate limiting or oscillatory solution.
Do not clip an invalid asymptotic result to one and present it as an exact transmission coefficient.

entries.title: Dimeric acidic-extractant stoichiometry and precision audit
entries.use_when: Liquid-liquid extraction data at two or more extractant concentrations and acidities must be used to infer a neutral metal complex, write the extraction reaction, calculate its equilibrium constant, or audit numbered statements.
steps: Use charge balance first: if singly charged A- is the only anionic ligand in a neutral extracted complex of M raised to z+, its deprotonated-ligand coefficient is z.

Let n be the number of H2A2 dimers consumed and write M raised to z+ plus n H2A2 as extracted complex M(A)z(HA)(2n-z) plus z H+; then D equals K times the dimer activity raised to n divided by hydrogen-ion activity raised to z.

For two conditions, calculate n from [ln(D1/D2) - z ln(H2/H1)] divided by ln(C1/C2), then map the near-integer n to the chemically admissible ligand counts without confusing dimer and monomer equivalents.
Calculate K independently from each condition as D times [H+] raised to z divided by [H2A2] raised to n, retaining guard digits and checking cross-condition consistency.

Evaluate reaction-coefficient sums, numerical inequalities, and reporting-precision statements separately; assign significant figures from the stated input precision, not from the scatter between K estimates.
guards: A radioactivity-count ratio represents the distribution ratio only when aliquot volumes and counting response are comparable.
Use equilibrium free-extractant concentration when extraction materially depletes the extractant; tracer-metal conditions often justify the initial concentration approximation.
Do not interpret the dimer concentration exponent as the number of monomeric HA ligands.
Do not round the slope before applying charge balance and aggregation-state constraints, and do not use replicate disagreement alone to reduce the significant figures supplied by the measurements.

entry.title: Coupled solubility and acid-base regression
entry.use_when: Solubility or precipitation is coupled to pH, buffering, or protonation of a dissolved ion, including multi-point measurements used to recover equilibrium constants or assess numerical choices.
steps: Write the solubility product, relevant acid-base equilibria, and mass balances together; distinguish free-ion concentrations from total dissolved concentration.
Derive the transformed linear model before fitting; for a 1:1 salt with a protonatable anion, fit squared solubility against hydrogen-ion concentration, with intercept Ksp and slope Ksp/Ka.
Transform every observation without rounding and compute ordinary least squares from centered sums, then recover physical constants algebraically and check positivity and residual quality.
Retain guard digits and accept a printed numerical choice only when the unrounded result lies within that choice's half-unit rounding interval at its displayed precision.
Evaluate every underlying statement independently before selecting any multiple-correct response.
guards: Do not replace a free-ion concentration with total solubility when protonation or complexation is present.
Do not regress directly against pH when the derived variable is hydrogen-ion concentration.
Do not estimate fitted coefficients from endpoints or use answer choices as regression targets.
Do not treat numerical proximity as valid rounding equivalence.

Check expected bounds and perform rounding only after evaluating the quotient.

Do not invert part and whole.
Do not convert to percent unless requested.
Do not print both fractional and percentage forms.

entry.title: Role-scoped temperatures and online answer provenance

steps: Assign every temperature, pressure, concentration, mass, and volume an explicit physical role before binding equations or tool arguments; textual proximity is not sufficient.

Treat retrieved knowledge and explicitly successful tool calls as supporting evidence. Check argument roles, units, physical bounds, and agreement with an independent derivation.
For online routes, record numeric values from the model's explicit final-answer line after evidence adjudication. Restrict legacy specialized synthesis to offline deterministic routes.
guards: Do not bind a quantity merely because it is nearest an apparatus noun.
Do not let a successful tool status substitute for validation of its arguments or scientific result.
